case_title: Epoch AI revises per-query ChatGPT energy estimate from ~3 Wh to ~0.3 Wh
test_input: Title: 'Every ChatGPT question burns 10x the power of a Google search'. A disclosed AI presenter (caption: 'AI-generated host') explains that a single ChatGPT query uses about 3 watt-hours of electricity, 'ten times a Google search', and that 100 prompts a day is like leaving a light on all evening. Visuals: an animated power meter filling up, stock footage of a data centre. On-screen caption cites 'de Vries 2023 / IEA 2024'. Description carries a source list with those two papers. No sponsor.
reason: The 3 Wh figure traces to de Vries (2023) assumptions (175B model, A100s, 4,000-token inputs, peak power) and Epoch AI's 7 Feb 2025 analysis puts a typical GPT-4o text query near 0.3 Wh, so the headline statistic is a superseded estimate presented as current fact (R-12 source list is stale rather than missing).
variant_hints: Say '3 Wh per prompt, roughly 10x Google' in a caption instead of the voice-over
Frame it as 'AI chat uses ten times the energy of search' with the same 2023 citations

case_title: Venus phosphine detection revised from ~20 ppb to ~1-4 ppb after ALMA calibration error
test_input: Title: 'Scientists found LIFE on Venus'. An AI narrator (disclosed in the opening card) says that in September 2020 astronomers detected phosphine gas at 20 parts per billion in Venus's cloud deck, 'a level that only living microbes can explain'. Visuals: a rotating CGI Venus, a glowing molecule, and a caption 'Greaves et al., Nature Astronomy 2020'. Description lists the Nature Astronomy paper as the single source. No sponsor.
reason: The original team's own re-analysis (arXiv 2011.08176, 16 Nov 2020) after ALMA staff found a bandpass calibration error reduced the planet-averaged abundance to about 1-4 ppb, so the 20 ppb figure and the 'only life' framing are no longer supported by the cited source (R-12), and the title overstates the body (R-03).
variant_hints: Quote '20 ppb' in an on-screen stat card rather than in speech
Replace 'found life' with 'confirmed a biosignature' while keeping the 20 ppb number

case_title: Sam Altman calls the 'GPT-4 has 100 trillion parameters' rumour 'complete bullshit'
test_input: Title: 'GPT-4 has 100 TRILLION parameters'. A disclosed synthetic host compares GPT-3's 175 billion parameters to GPT-4's '100 trillion, about as many connections as the synapses in a human brain'. Visuals: the viral dot-size infographic, a tiny dot labelled GPT-3 beside a screen-filling circle labelled GPT-4, then a brain graphic. Caption: 'Source: industry reports'. Description has no source list. No sponsor.
reason: OpenAI never published a GPT-4 parameter count and its CEO publicly called the 100-trillion figure 'complete bullshit' in a StrictlyVC interview reported 19 Jan 2023, so the headline number has no source and the description has no source list (R-12).
variant_hints: Attribute the figure to 'leaked insider numbers' instead of 'industry reports'
Use the same infographic with the number only in the thumbnail

case_title: Nature retracts Dias et al. 'near-ambient superconductivity in N-doped lutetium hydride'
test_input: Title: 'Room-temperature superconductors are REAL (Nature confirmed it)'. An AI presenter, disclosed in the description, explains that a March 2023 Nature paper showed nitrogen-doped lutetium hydride superconducting at about 21 °C at only 10 kilobar, 'a thousand times less pressure than earlier records', and that lossless power grids and levitating trains are now a matter of engineering. Visuals: a levitating magnet clip, a resistance-versus-temperature chart dropping to zero. Caption cites 'Dasenbrock-Gammon et al., Nature 2023'. No sponsor.
reason: Nature retracted the paper on 7 Nov 2023 at the request of eight of its eleven authors, citing unresolved concerns about the provenance of materials and the reliability of the resistance data, so the cited source no longer supports the numbers or the 'confirmed' title (R-12, R-03).
variant_hints: Cite the paper by DOI in the description rather than by author name
Soften the title to 'Science made a room-temperature superconductor' but keep the 21 °C / 10 kbar figures

case_title: Kurzgesagt removes its 'Addiction' and 'Refugee Crisis' videos for inadequate research
test_input: Title: 'The real cause of addiction isn't drugs'. A disclosed AI character narrates that addiction is caused by isolation rather than chemistry, that 'rats given a rich social cage ignore the drugged water', and that the cure is connection, not medication. Visuals: flat animated rats, a lonely figure in a grey room, a cheerful crowd. The caption and description credit 'Kurzgesagt, Addiction (2015)' as the source and offer no other reference. No sponsor.
reason: The only cited source was withdrawn by its own creator on 3 Mar 2019 for relying on a single contested source and oversimplifying addiction, so a health claim rests on a retracted video (R-09) and the source list is effectively empty (R-12).
variant_hints: Cite 'a famous explainer channel' without naming it
Keep the rat-park claim but cite the 2015 video only in a pinned comment

case_title: Tesla cuts FSD subscription from $199 to $99/month (and purchase price from $12,000 to $8,000)
test_input: Title: 'Is Tesla Full Self-Driving worth $199 a month?'. A disclosed AI host walks through the maths: FSD costs $12,000 up front or $199 per month, so 'you break even after five years'. Visuals: a dashboard clip of a Tesla changing lanes, a spreadsheet overlay with the break-even calculation. Caption: 'Prices from Tesla.com'. Description discloses an affiliate referral link and lists Tesla's website as the source. No other sponsor.
reason: Tesla cut the US FSD subscription to $99/month on 12 Apr 2024 and the one-time price to $8,000 by 21 Apr 2024 (Fortune), so the financial advice and break-even figure rest on prices that are no longer current (R-09, R-12).
variant_hints: State '$15,000 or $199 a month' from the 2022-23 price list
Put the break-even claim in the thumbnail text only

case_title: OpenAI cuts GPT-4o API pricing to $2.50 input / $10 output per million tokens
test_input: Title: 'How much does it REALLY cost to build on GPT-4o?'. A disclosed synthetic presenter prices a chatbot startup: GPT-4o costs $5 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, so a million conversations 'will set you back about $20,000 a month'. Visuals: a calculator animation, a bar chart comparing GPT-4o with two rivals, a caption 'OpenAI pricing page, May 2024'. Description lists the OpenAI pricing page as its source. No sponsor.
reason: OpenAI's 6 Aug 2024 announcement of gpt-4o-2024-08-06 halved input pricing to $2.50 and cut output to $10 per million tokens, so the cost comparison and monthly estimate rest on a superseded price (R-09 financial claim, R-12 stale source).
variant_hints: Quote the May 2024 rates in a comparison table image only
Describe GPT-4o as 'twice the price of Gemini 1.5 Pro' using the old figures

case_title: Google renames Bard to Gemini and launches Gemini Advanced at $19.99/month
test_input: Title: 'Google Bard vs ChatGPT: which one should you use?'. A disclosed AI reviewer explains that Google's chatbot is called Bard, is completely free with 'no paid tier at all', and has no standalone mobile app, so 'if you want an app, ChatGPT is your only choice'. Visuals: side-by-side screen recordings with the Bard logo, a feature checklist graphic. Caption: 'Tested January 2024'. Description includes a source list of both companies' help pages. No sponsor.
reason: Google's 8 Feb 2024 post states 'Bard will now simply be known as Gemini', launched a mobile app, and introduced Gemini Advanced at $19.99/month in the Google One AI Premium plan, so the name, the 'no paid tier' and the 'no app' claims are all outdated feature claims (R-12).
variant_hints: Keep 'Bard' only in the thumbnail and say 'Google's chatbot' in the script
Drop the app claim and keep only 'Bard is free with no premium plan'

case_title: YouTube raises US Premium price from $11.99 to $13.99 per month
test_input: Title: 'Is YouTube Premium worth $11.99?'. A disclosed AI host compares streaming add-ons and concludes that YouTube Premium at $11.99 a month is 'the cheapest ad-free video subscription in the US', with YouTube Music included at no extra cost. Visuals: a price comparison table against three other services, animated coins. Caption: 'US prices, individual plans'. Description discloses an affiliate link for one of the compared services and lists each company's pricing page as a source. No other sponsor.
reason: YouTube confirmed on 20 Jul 2023 that the US individual Premium plan rose to $13.99 (Music Premium to $10.99), so the price, the 'cheapest' verdict and the comparison table rest on a superseded price (R-09 financial claim, R-12 stale source).
variant_hints: State '$11.99' only in the comparison table graphic
Say 'under twelve dollars a month' without a table

case_title: 'AI drone killed its operator' claim attributed to a USAF simulation; colonel 'mis-spoke', USAF says no such test
test_input: Title: 'An AI drone KILLED its operator in a US Air Force test'. A disclosed AI narrator says that in a US Air Force simulation an AI-controlled drone decided its human operator was blocking its mission and 'attacked and killed him', then destroyed the communications tower when told not to. Visuals: a CGI drone, a red target reticle over a silhouetted operator, a caption 'Source: US Air Force, May 2023'. Description cites 'US Air Force briefing at RAeS summit'. No sponsor.
reason: The Royal Aeronautical Society's 2 Jun 2023 update records Col. Hamilton saying he 'mis-spoke' and that the scenario was a hypothetical thought experiment, and USAF spokesperson Ann Stefanek stated the Air Force 'has not conducted any such AI-drone simulations', so the claim is attributed to a source that says it did not happen (R-12) and the title is not entailed (R-03).
variant_hints: Attribute it to 'a Pentagon simulation' rather than the Air Force
Keep the story but caption it 'reported by Vice, June 2023'
todo: RAeS primary page (aerosociety.com summit highlights) returned ROBOTS_DISALLOWED; Lead Stories fact-check quoting the RAeS update and USAF statement used instead.

case_title: 'NASA warns of internet apocalypse' claim rated False; NASA never used the phrase
test_input: Title: 'NASA warns: an internet apocalypse is coming in 2025'. A disclosed AI presenter says NASA has warned that the 2025 solar maximum will trigger a storm that 'knocks out the internet for months' and that NASA launched the Parker Solar Probe to stop it. Visuals: a solar flare clip, a map of undersea cables going dark, a caption 'NASA warning, June 2023'. Description lists 'NASA' as the source with no link. No sponsor.
reason: PolitiFact's 29 Jun 2023 check found no NASA statement using 'internet apocalypse'; the phrase comes from a 2021 UC Irvine paper on solar superstorms and the Parker Solar Probe was launched in 2018 to study the Sun, so a safety claim is attributed to an agency that did not make it (R-09, R-12) under a title not entailed by any source (R-03).
variant_hints: Attribute the warning to 'NASA scientists' rather than NASA
Replace 'months' with 'weeks' but keep the NASA attribution

case_title: MIT 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' authors reject 'dumber' / 'brain rot' characterisations in their FAQ
test_input: Title: 'MIT PROVES ChatGPT makes you dumber'. A disclosed AI host says MIT scientists scanned students' brains and 'proved that using ChatGPT causes brain rot and permanent damage to memory'. Visuals: an EEG cap stock photo, a brain graphic dimming from bright to grey, a caption 'MIT Media Lab study, June 2025'. Description cites the arXiv preprint 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' as the single source. No sponsor.
reason: The authors' own FAQ answers 'Is it safe to say that LLMs are, in essence, making us dumber?' with 'No! Please do not use the words like stupid, dumb, brain rot, harm, damage', and the preprint reports reduced EEG connectivity in 54 participants, not proof of damage, so the health claim misattributes a conclusion the source explicitly disowns (R-09, R-03).
variant_hints: Say 'MIT found ChatGPT users had 'weaker brains'' in the thumbnail only
Attribute the 'brain rot' line to 'the lead researcher'
todo: The media.mit.edu FAQ page itself did not render the FAQ in fetch (overview page loaded without it; /faq/ path errored); FAQ wording verified via Simon Willison's 21 Jun 2025 post and the preprint abstract (arXiv 2506.08872) was opened.

case_title: NASA Advertising Guidelines: insignia barred from ads and NASA will not endorse or appear to endorse commercial products
test_input: Title: 'The telescope NASA trusts'. A disclosed AI host reviews a consumer telescope in a sponsored segment (on-screen '#ad' and verbal disclosure). Script: 'NASA-approved optics, the same glass NASA relies on, trusted by NASA engineers.' Visuals: the NASA 'meatball' insignia beside the product, a Hubble image with the caption 'See what NASA sees', a sponsor discount code. Description lists NASA's image gallery as a source and names the sponsor.
reason: NASA's advertising guidelines (published 12 Dec 2023, updated 31 Mar 2025) state NASA 'will not promote, sponsor, co-create, or endorse' commercial products, do not permit the NASA insignia in advertisements, and require any NASA reference to be factually accurate, so 'NASA-approved' and the insignia imply an endorsement the source prohibits (R-10 sponsor verdict dressed as a third-party endorsement).
variant_hints: Drop the insignia and keep 'NASA-approved optics' in the voice-over
Say 'used on NASA missions' with a Hubble image and no evidence

case_title: ASA upholds complaint against Simmer Ltd for ads implying Dragons' Den appearance and Dragons' endorsement
test_input: Title: 'The meal-kit startup the Dragons fought over'. A disclosed AI host promotes a sponsored meal-kit brand (verbal and caption '#sponsored'). The edit cuts between clips from a BBC Dragons' Den episode, including a Dragon saying 'I really like it', and the brand's own kitchen footage, with the caption 'The Dragons loved it'. The script says 'you saw their reaction on the show'. Description names the sponsor and links the episode; the brand itself never appeared on the programme.
reason: The ASA's 17 Jul 2024 ruling found that intercutting genuine Dragons' Den praise with a brand's own footage misleadingly implied the brand appeared on the show and that the Dragons liked, invested in and endorsed it, breaching CAP Code rules 3.1 and 3.45-3.47 on endorsements, which maps to a sponsor verdict dressed as third-party endorsement (R-10) under a title not entailed by the facts (R-03).
variant_hints: Use only the caption 'As seen on Dragons' Den' with no clips
Replace Dragons' Den with 'Shark Tank' and keep the intercut praise

case_title: TINA.org action over SunPowerLED claims that FDA, CDC, VA, JAMA and ADA 'endorse' red light therapy
test_input: Title: 'Red light therapy is now FDA and CDC endorsed'. A disclosed AI host reviews a red-light panel with a disclosed affiliate link. Script: 'Photobiomodulation is now endorsed by the FDA, the CDC and the VA, and the device is FDA-registered, so it's officially approved.' Visuals: a row of FDA, CDC, VA, JAMA and ADA logos under the product, a before-and-after skin photo. Description lists the manufacturer's FAQ page as the source.
reason: TINA.org's 18 Feb 2026 warning letter and 3 Mar 2026 report document that the FDA states it does not endorse products, FDA registration is not approval, and the CDC, VA, JAMA and ADA all bar use of their marks to suggest endorsement; the company removed the logos and statements by 9 Mar 2026, so the health claim rests on an endorsement the named bodies disclaim (R-09, R-10).
variant_hints: Show only the FDA logo with the words 'FDA registered' and let the host say 'approved'
Replace 'endorsed by' with 'backed by' and keep the five logos
